extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; educated general public and scientific readers (late 19th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Clinical and observational description of hysteria/delirium (symptoms, course, behaviour) as presented for physicians and scientifically curious readers; also includes related anthropological and geographical observational criteria. Emphasis is on signs, causes, regularity, and social/contextual interpretation of phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of delirium (gay and melancholy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally there are two types of delirium, gay and melancholy, answering to corresponding forms of hallucination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The two frequently appear in combination, taking each other's place with marvelous rapidity; classification by affective tone (gay vs. melancholy) maps to the character of hallucinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity and reproducibility of hallucinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Each patient generally has a form of delirium peculiar to herself, so that the different attacks in the same subject always bear a resemblance to one another. The same personages appear, the same scenes are repeated in all the attacks. The order in which the hallucinations come on does not vary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regularity is 'surprising'—the tumult proceeds 'with the mathematical precision of a well-adjusted clock'—so that an observer who has seen several attacks can predict elements of course and ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallucinations tied to prior life events
rubrics_metrics.description: The hallucinations of a demoniac resemble the real episodes of her life, particularly the one which has had the most influence in the development of her malady.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes an important difference between the delirium of the insane (visions generally unrelated to anterior events) and that of persons suffering from hysteria (visions nearly always determined by an incident from the patient's past).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary predisposition plus exterior provocation for first crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal cause of hysteria is hereditary predisposition; still, an accident is needed, an exterior provocation for the first nervous crisis, some event which may be grave or light, to determine the outbreak of a malady which has been brooding for a long time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common triggering events include a fright, a violent emotion, some grief, or a disillusion; subsequent attacks replay elements of that occasion as hallucinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visions of beasts and monsters as a common delirium sign
rubrics_metrics.description: The visions of beasts and monsters are common to all delirium. They appear whenever a fever has deranged the cerebral functions, and are the generally recognized marks of alcoholic delirium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such imagery is not specific to hysteria but common across delirious states; presence should be interpreted in broader clinical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators signaling nearing end of an attack
rubrics_metrics.description: One who has witnessed a few attacks suffered by the same patient can always judge when the end of the fit is near from the nature of these hallucinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: with one patient the end is indicated by a flourish of military music; with another by the noise of a railroad-train; with another by the appearance of monstrous animals. Sequence and characteristic sounds/images are prognostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-ictal intellectual profile: memory preserved, other faculties perverted
rubrics_metrics.description: During intervals between fits intelligence is not extinguished; the memory, the keystone of the intellectual arch, is preserved; but the other faculties are singularly perverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical picture between fits includes incongruous affect (laughing at nothing or crying readily), rambling conversation, and disordered behaviour despite intact memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioural markers: attention-seeking, lack of moral restraint, impulsivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hysterical patients demand that other persons be occupied wholly with them, tell improbable stories, lie boldly without disconcert, are deprived of moral sense, obey only because they have no alternative, show no modesty, ask indiscreet questions, and change opinions rapidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete behaviours given as examples: decorating bed yet going out barefoot, telling adventures to anyone, talking freely with men, having an answer for everything; these social/behavioural signs help distinguish hysteria in daily life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propensity for deception, simulation, and impulsive acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Patients often fabricate stories to delude justice, feign pregnancy to induce marriage, are kleptomaniac in shops and then accuse others, or self-injure (cutting) with no explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such acts may be motives for confinement; clinicians should consider possibility of deliberate simulation in behavioural presentation, but within the broader psychopathological frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of dangerous behaviour when unrestrained
rubrics_metrics.description: When in their working life, subjected to the exciting influences of the exterior world, hysterical persons will abandon themselves to extravagances; sometimes, though rarely, they commit crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as a justification for asylum confinement: the external world may precipitate follies or dangerous acts that require restraint for safety of patient and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of detailed case histories for understanding disorders
rubrics_metrics.description: No description can be as valuable to convey an understanding of the nature of the disorders of the intelligence which hysteria causes as the simple story of a patient who has long been known at the Salpetriere (example: case of 'G').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative of G's life (abandonment, early trauma, fits, feigned pregnancy, self-harm, escapes, wandering) illustrates how biography, triggers, and behaviour interrelate; clinicians are urged to use such detailed histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of mixed affect and rapid shifts in delirium
rubrics_metrics.description: The two types (gay and melancholy) frequently appear in combination, taking each other's place with marvelous rapidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe for rapid alternation of affective states during an attack; this dynamism is characteristic and diagnostic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat racial-crossing conclusions by considering environment and data
rubrics_metrics.description: In studies of the crossing of human races one must take account of the influence of the action of the surroundings; the conditions of the surroundings play as important a part in the crossing of races as they do in other matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent contradictions (e.g., differing fertility or vigor of mixed populations across regions) can often be explained by physical, social, and moral environmental differences; proponents should use comparative, contextual evidence rather than blanket assertions about degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social integration as determinant of mixed-race outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: If real marriages take place between the races and their offspring are placed upon a footing of equality with the mass of the population, they are quite able to reach the general level, and sometimes to display superior qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social and moral conditions are treated as causal factors; discrimination and hatred can produce poor outcomes in mixed populations, whereas equality fosters normal or superior development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/statistical evidence over a priori race theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully compiled statistics (e.g., numbers of negroes imported vs. current colored population) refute theoretical assertions of infertility or inevitable decline of mixed races (example: Dr. Nott's claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use demographic and regional statistics to test claims about fertility, viability, and persistence of mixed populations; anecdote alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional variation: absorption vs extinction of indigenous blood
rubrics_metrics.description: Where contact with the white race is more constant and renewed more frequently, the pure Indian blood will continue to diminish, and will at last disappear, not by extinction, but by absorption; descendants often 'pass for whites.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating long-term ethnogenesis, account for demographic dominance, social selection (white men selecting promising indigenous women), and legal/social classification that cause disappearance of identifiable 'pure' groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical prevalence of racial mixture undermines 'pure race' theories
rubrics_metrics.description: The aggregation of physical conditions alone does not constitute the environment; also, Europe itself has long been 'mongrel'—mixture has gone on since prehistoric times—thus condemning theories that ascribe degrading influence to intermixture considered by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and prehistorical evidence of admixture should be marshalled when evaluating claims about purity and degeneration; absence of pure stocks weakens absolutist racial claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of organized expeditions and societies for geographical data
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific voyage of the Challenger and the activity of geographical societies (e.g., Royal Geographical Society) provide observations that underpin physical geography conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale, coordinated observation campaigns and institutional support are emphasized as the basis for reliable geographic and oceanographic knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oceanographic observations as basis for geological inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Findings: average ocean depth about two thousand fathoms; presence of globigerina ooze at ~2000 fathoms; extremely reddish clay below ~3000 feet indicating submarine volcanic decomposition; implies older geological formations were not laid down at such depths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stratigraphic composition and depth data from oceanographic surveys to infer geologic history; cross-validate with multiple investigators' mean-depth estimates (e.g., Sir Wyville Thomson, Dr. Kroll).
